fact_text: As an EU/EEA national (France is an EU/EEA member state), a French citizen does NOT need a residence permit or work permit to live and work in Norway — Norway is an EEA member (not EU), and free movement applies under the EEA Agreement.
evidence_quote: Nationals of EU/EEA countries do not need a residence permit to stay or work in Norway. However, all nationals of EU/EEA countries who want to stay for longer than three months must register with the police.

fact_text: Non-obvious flag: registration is done with the POLICE (politiet), not the immigration directorate, and is mandatory when staying longer than three months. Nordic citizens are exempt, but French nationals are not.
evidence_quote: all nationals of EU/EEA countries who want to stay for longer than three months must register with the police.

fact_text: The registration certificate (registreringsbevis) is the document confirming the police have registered the EU/EEA national as living in Norway.
evidence_quote: A registration certificate is a document confirming that the police have registered you as an EU/EEA national living in Norway.

fact_text: Non-obvious flag: the registration certificate is NOT proof of right of residence and does not need to be renewed — you register only once regardless of length of stay. Right of residence is documented separately (e.g. employment contract, pay slips).
evidence_quote: The registration certificate is not a document that confirms your right of residence in Norway.

fact_text: When registering as an EU/EEA citizen, the mover must ALSO apply to the Tax Administration for a Norwegian identification number and a tax deduction card — immigration, residence and tax steps are chained together.
evidence_quote: When you apply for registration as an EU/EEA citizen, you must also apply for a Norwegian identification number (external website) and tax deduction card (external website) from the Tax Administration.

fact_text: An employee intending to stay in Norway for at least six months consecutively must report a move to Norway (folkeregistrering) to the National Population Register at Skatteetaten.
evidence_quote: If you intend to stay in Norway for at least six months consecutively or more permanently, you must report a move to Norway.

fact_text: A national identity number (personnummer / fodselsnummer) is issued once a move to Norway is approved and the person is registered as resident — you cannot apply for it directly; the National Population Register determines eligibility.
evidence_quote: You cannot apply for a national identity number. It is the National Population Register that will determine whether you meet the conditions for being issued a national identity number.

fact_text: Registering a move to Norway requires an in-person ID check and documentation proving the stay will last at least six months.
evidence_quote: You must undergo an ID check, and you’ll be asked to provide documentation showing that you’ll be living in Norway for at least 6 months.

fact_text: Non-obvious flag: a D-number is a TEMPORARY identification number for those who do not meet the requirements for a national identity number (e.g. working in Norway for a few months) — it is distinct from the permanent personnummer.
evidence_quote: A Norwegian D number is an identification number that may be relevant for those who do not meet the requirements for a national identity number.

fact_text: An individual cannot apply for a D-number themselves — an enterprise or authority (e.g. the employer, Tax Administration, a bank, or Nav) requests it when it needs the person to have a Norwegian identification number.
evidence_quote: You cannot apply for a D number. An enterprise or authority can request a D number when it needs you to have a Norwegian identification number.

fact_text: For EEA citizens specifically, Nav can request a D-number when they are applying for jobs and/or receiving national insurance benefits — linking the residence-ID step to the social-security step.
evidence_quote: Nav – for citizens of EEA countries who are applying for jobs and/or receiving national insurance benefits.

fact_text: Most people who work in Norway must have a tax deduction card (skattekort) and a Norwegian identification number (D-number or national identity number) — the tax card is required for payroll.
evidence_quote: Most people who work in Norway must have a tax deduction card and a Norwegian identification number (D number or national identity number).

fact_text: Non-obvious flag: when a newly-arrived worker applies for a tax deduction card, they are AUTOMATICALLY enrolled in the voluntary PAYE (Pay As You Earn) scheme by default, taxed at a fixed percentage deducted by the employer.
evidence_quote: When you’re new in Norway and apply for a tax deduction card, you’ll automatically join a voluntary tax scheme called PAYE (Pay As You Earn).

fact_text: Under the PAYE scheme the worker pays a flat 25 percent tax on salary (or 17.4 percent in 2026 if exempt from Norwegian national insurance contributions); tax is deducted at source and no tax return is issued.
evidence_quote: When you’re part of the PAYE scheme, you pay 25 percent tax on your salary. If you’re exempted from paying national insurance contributions in Norway, you pay 17.4 percent tax in 2026.

fact_text: The PAYE scheme has an income ceiling: it can only be used when annual earnings are below NOK 725,050 in 2026 (the 2025 threshold was NOK 697,150). Above that, the worker must use the general taxation rules.
evidence_quote: You can join the PAYE scheme when you: earn less than NOK 725,050 in 2026. For 2025 the threshold amount was NOK 697,150.

fact_text: Norwegian tax residency turns on the 183/270-day rule: short work stays under 183 days in a 12-month period (or under 270 days in a 36-month period) mean the worker re-joins PAYE each time they apply for a tax card rather than becoming tax resident.
evidence_quote: If you travel to Norway for short work stays (less than 183 days in a 12-month period or less than 270 days in a 36-month period), you'll join the PAYE scheme every time you apply for a tax deduction card.

fact_text: A worker who has been a tax resident in Norway for more than one year can no longer use the PAYE scheme and must be assessed under the general taxation rules (with a tax return and eligible deductions).
evidence_quote: You cannot join the PAYE scheme when you: earn more than NOK 725,050 during the year (applies to the 2026 income year). For the 2025 income year, the threshold amount is NOK 697,150. have been a tax resident in Norway for more than a year

fact_text: An EU/EEA employee who is resident and works in Norway is enrolled as a member of the Norwegian National Insurance Scheme (folketrygden / trygd) — membership is automatic on residence plus employment.
evidence_quote: If you are resident and work in Norway, you will be enrolled as a member of the Norwegian National Insurance Scheme.

fact_text: National Insurance membership means the worker is covered for essential healthcare expenses from the national health service but still pays standard user fees (egenandel) for treatment.
evidence_quote: This means that you will be covered for essential expenses for healthcare services from the national health service and that you will have to pay user fees for any treatment you receive.

fact_text: EU/EEA social-security coordination (Reg. 883/2004 applied via the EEA Agreement): dependent family members living in another EU/EEA country than the worker are entitled to have healthcare expenses reimbursed, documented via an S1 certificate applied for at Helfo.
evidence_quote: If you have dependent family members who live in Switzerland or another EU/EEA country than where you live, they will also have the right to be reimbursed for health care expenses.

fact_text: The S1 certificate for family members is issued by Helfo and only becomes valid once the National Insurance authorities in the family's country of residence (e.g. France) confirm registration; Helfo's processing time is normally up to 4 weeks.
evidence_quote: You or your family members must submit certificate S1 to the National Insurance authorities in the country in which your dependents live. The form will not be valid until Helfo has received feedback from the National Insurance authorities in your country of residence.

fact_text: Every person registered in the National Population Register as resident in a Norwegian municipality has the right to a regular GP (fastlege); the municipality is responsible for providing GP services.
evidence_quote: All inhabitants who are registered in the National Population Register as living in Norway have the right to a General Practitioner/family doctor.

fact_text: CRITICAL non-obvious flag: people who hold only a D-number are NOT entitled to a fastlege (regular GP) — the right to a GP attaches to residence registration (personnummer), not to a D-number. Narrow exceptions apply (asylum seekers, NATO personnel, foreign representatives).
evidence_quote: Persons who have D-numbers are not entitled to a GP, the only exceptions are the following groups, who are entitled to a GP: Asylum seekers with D-numbers, and their families NATO personnel with D-numbers and their families Foreign personnel sent as representatives to Norway and their families

fact_text: Even without a GP, D-number holders remain entitled to necessary medical treatment, which the municipality is responsible for providing.
evidence_quote: Other persons with a D-number are not entitled to a GP, but are entitled necessary medical treatment.

fact_text: Emergency and out-of-hours care access: for acute illness outside GP opening hours contact the out-of-hours medical service (legevakt) on 116 117; for life-threatening emergencies call 113.
evidence_quote: In the event of acute injury or illness outside of the GP’s opening hours, you must contact the out-of-hours medical services, legevakten (116 117). In life-threatening emergency, call 113.

fact_text: A member of the Norwegian National Insurance Scheme is entitled to a European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) issued by Norway, usable in any EU/EEA country except Norway (e.g. when visiting France).
evidence_quote: You are entitled to a European Health Insurance Card from Norway. You may use this card in any EU/EEA country except for Norway.

fact_text: As an EEA citizen, a French national has the right to come to Norway and receive planned healthcare within the specialised health service.
evidence_quote: As an EEA citizen you have the right to come to Norway and receive planned healthcare within the specialised health service here.
